Dr Alessandro Andreone's new invention [5282]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Dr Alessandro Andreone

There are very few statistics but it is estimated that there are between 10 000 – 13 000 people that are burnt in KZN every year.

About 6 000 – 7000 of them need hospital admission. Inkhosi Albert Lithuli has the only dedicated burns unit and they can only treat 700 patients a year.

What happens to the other 5000 patients.

Dr Alessandro Andreone has been working in the burns unit for 8 years now.

For most people the doctors are able to do a skin graft when a patient comes in with burn wounds. However there are some that come in with burns that are so extensive that they do not have enough skin on their body to cover the area.

In overseas countries they rely on cadaver skin. Nikki Allorto who works at Edendale Hospital also looks after wounds at her hospital but there are cultural reasons why the idea of a skin bank has not taken traction.

Dr Andreone has been grappling with trying to devise new methods of reducing the time that patients stay in the burns unit to make way for new patients.

Recently Carte Blanche featured “Pippie” Kruger the three-year-old burn victim from Limpopo who has made front-page headlines over the past month because of a ¬revolutionary skin transplant operation for which the skin was grown from her own cells in a laboratory in the United States. It was the first time the procedure was performed in Africa.

The cost of this technology was approximately a R 1 000 000 and according to Dr Andreone the results are not very successful as the epithelial layer is very thin and it can break. Especially in areas of high friction.

Liboy is a labourer in KZN. He was leaving work with his toolbox and 3 men approached him and attacked him to steal his toolbox. Before they left him they lit his clothes on fire and left him to burn. Luckily he was only 2 km away from his employers residence and walked there with 70 % burns on his body. They rushed him to Albert Lithuli.

Luckily Dr Andreone was on duty. They removed the burnt flesh and had to put a steralising layer of bovine collagen to protect the exposed flesh. Dr Looking for an alternative way to treat patients, Andreone is Italian and had been researching medical journals and found two machines in Italy that he wanted to experiment with.

The machines were not designed for burns applications but he thought that they may be able to work.
In Liboy’s case he had enough flesh to create a mesh to cover most of his chest. But how could they get the skin to grow in the holes of the mesh.

The Vivostat is a machine that is used in neurosurgery and it extracts fibren from the platelet rich plasma it can extract from blood. This is used to stop bleeding or leaking in brain operations.

The Rigenera machine is something that looks like a small electric blender. In a saline solution the doctor places about 2 cm squared of skin into the jug. This blends it so that the skin cells breaks down.

Dr Andreone took these cells and put them in the platelet rich plasma and sprayed the mixture onto Liboy’s wounds.

To his surprise the wounds started healing very quickly. A process that should have taken 2 months took as little as two weeks.

Mr Naidoo was working on his car over the weekend and he did not realise that there was a petrol spill and the petrol had spilt onto the bottom of his pants. He lit a cigarette and his pants caught on fire burning virtually all the skin off his feet. He was rushed to a regional hospital but although they dressed his wounds he was unable to get proper treatment for 2 months.

It is obvious how painful burn wounds are.

Eventually because his wounds were not healing he was transferred to Albert Lithuli and Dr Andreone tried his new method on him. Withing a couple of weeks the wounds had healed completely.
(There is still scar tissue but they are not open weeping wounds).

Dr Andreone has treated 8 patients with this method and it seems to be working very well. They have submitted a paper in the Internation Burns Journal and it will be published in 6 weeks time.

Both case studies are willing to talk to us.
I can interview Dr Andreone, his boss Dr Daan den Hollander and an independent person who has looked at the work.
They have also been nominated for a provincial award for the most inventive new medical technique.

This method does not only reduce the time that the patient takes to heal, the cost in comparison to epithelial cell culture is a lot less. By getting more patients out of the unit quicker they weill be able to see more patients.

What was also interesting was that all of the patients were not there for paraffin burns or accidents as I had imagined, they were all victims of assault where someone had deliberately tried to burn them.







Case Study:
Sipho Ndlele
LeeBoy Arendse

Expert:
Dr. Alessandro Andreone
Dr. Nikki Allorto

Press Release:


Saving Burn Victims
It’s estimated that in KwaZulu-Natal, around 7000 people suffer life-threatening burn injuries every year. But provincial State healthcare can only treat a few hundred victims every month. Now a new procedure that sprays skin cells and platelet rich plasma onto burn injuries could mean more patients can be treated in a shorter period of time. Carte Blanche explores this game-changing medical treatment.
Producer: Carol Albertyn Christie
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


Burns Script


V/O
It’s estimated that in KwaZulu-Natal, around 7000 people suffer life-threatening burn injuries every year. But state healthcare can only treat a few hundred VICTIMS. Now, a new procedure developed here in South Africa, can treat more patients in a shorter period of time.

Link
We have one of the highest rates of burn victims in the world. We are at the Inkosi Albert Luthuli Hospital where we are watching a fascinating process which helps to heal the patient in half the time of traditional methods.

V/O
This is the brain child of Dr Alessandro Andreone, who has developed what could be described as a world first, a spray on skin with the patient’s own skin cells. This method has won a provincial award for the most inventive new medical technique.

Dr Andreone
“We spray these epithelial cells , mixed with plasma over the wounds and then we expose 5 days later and we got these amazing results.”

Mac
“What were those results?”

Dr Andreone
“The graft not only took 100% also it start to close. At the beginning we were very surprised. We are not thinking to have this result straight away.”

V/O
LeeBoy Arendse was Dr Andreone’s first patient. In October last year he stopped in at his local spaza in Durban on his way home from work. He only had R50 on him and bought a cooldrink and a pack of cigarettes.

LeeBoy
“As I was walking there was somebody who was following me, the one from behind grabbed me and choking me. I let go of the mineral (cooldrink) ,
I was trying to get this one’s hand off my neck. They took the change, and my phone and the one at the back said that let me dala him, let me dala him.

V/O
Although they had a knife, the attackers decided to spray him with a colourless liquid.


LeeBoy
He was pouring me with something. I thought it was maybe water. He threw a matchstick on me. Boom. I caught alight.

V/O
Once the attackers had fled, Leeboy managed to walk about 500m back to his employer’s house.

Link
Leeboy was rushed to Inkhosi Albert Lithuli Hospital,he had sustained 50% full thickness burns all over his body. His life hung in the balance.

V/O
Dr Andreone was born in Italy but has been working at Albert Luthuli for over a decade. He attended to LeeBoy on his arrival.

Dr Andreone
“When he come down here his condition there were really, really critical, we excised nearly 45% of all of is full thickness burns, it was so deep we went up to the bone.”

V/O
Luckily LeeBoy managed to get the medical care he needed, but many others aren’t as lucky.

V/O
Dr Nikki Allorto is a Specialist Surgeon at Edendale Hospital and President of the Pan African Burn Society.

Mac
“So Nikki what are the burn stats in South Africa, how serious is the problem?”

Nikki
“More serious than most people realise.Few years ago when I travelled around the country looking and visiting each burn unit, we were looking at 8000 admissions per year. and that’s only the bigger burn units its not the private health care and its not the smaller burn units”

Andreone
“The problem here in Kwa Zulu Natal is that we got huge burn, the burn that I am talking about is more than 25% of total body surface that is burned. Probably 5000 of them they are supposed to receive special care.’

Mac
“Doctor you said that you can treat 500 patients a year. What happens to the others?”

Andreone
“Ja, that is a really good question. We try to do is we try to visit the other hospital on a regular basis. Along the line I think we are loosing a few of them.”

V/O
Realising the tremendous need for care Dr Andreone has been grappling with finding a way of reducing the time that patients stay in the burns unit, so that they can make way for new patients.

V/O
There are 3 different grades of burn. 1st degree and 2nd degree burns don’t usually need hopsitalisation. But when one is burnt like LeeBoy was, with 3rd degree or full thickness burns, surgery is definitely required.

Nikki
“That type of burn needs surgery, so we need to cut off the tissue that is dead we need to do skin grafting and this comes from the patients own skin.”

V/O
Although spray on skin was developed by Australian doctors in the mid 90’s, they used water as a medium.
Through intensive research Dr Andreone found an unusual solution.
His procedure, the first of its kind in the world, allows for skin cells to be “airbrushed” with a product made from the patients own blood instead of water.

Link
LeeBoy was the first that burn specialist Dr Andreone with a ground breaking procedure that saved his life.

V/O
Andreone’s new technique has caused a lot of interest world wide.

On a conference in Italy, he saw two machines that were designed for other medical uses and realised that if he used them together, it might quicken the skin’s healing process.
Once the patient is sedated, 120 ml of blood is taken and placed in a machine called the Vivostat and from that a sticky, glue like substance called Plasma Rich Fibrine, is extracted.

Link
The process that is happening right now is the blood is being heated to about 36 degrees, its then that it starts separating and the platelets will be going into a syringe that is inside the machine. I think we can almost start hearing it now. Because it does say it’s ready.

V/O
While that is taking place, Dr Andreone cut a 2 square centimetre piece of skin from Leeboy.

Link
So as you can imagine this is a painstaking process. The doctor is taking very very small and he has put them under 195 blades and those blades will then give him a solution and that solution he will then use as part of the skin grafting process.

V/O
Many burn victims have to fight to survive and LeeBoy’s case was no different. He stopped breathing during the operation and to save him Dr Andreone had to perform an emergency tracheotomy.

Mac
“At some point you had to be resuccitated in theatre. What happened?”

LeeBoy
‘I think I crushed. I died. Then Andreone performed his miracles now I’m back.”

Mac
“So he basically brought you back to life?”

LeeBoy
“Yes.”

V/O
To make the grafted skin stretch further, it is rolled through a mesh machine and it stretches out like fish net stockings.
Dr Andreone then mixes the solution of skin cells with the Platelet Rich Fibrine and then sprays it onto the skin mesh areas.
He says his method not only reduces scarring but the skin also has added elasticity. This is what LeeBoy looks like now.

Andreone
“We did one case, better to see if it will happen again.”

V/O
Sipho Ndlela is another success story of Dr Andreone’s spray skin method.
He is a panel beater by trade. In June friends asked him to help start their broken down car. They had a petrol pipe straight into the carburetor.

Sipho
“By the time the car say brrm brrm, I pressed the accelerator and it saw boof. After that burn I did not see nothing.”

V/O
The petrol bottle exploded underneath him. Engulfed in flames his friends dragged him out of the front windscreen and rushed him to hospital.



Andreone
“Sipho was severe burns he had more than 70 – 75% of deep partial to full thickness burns.

V/O
Sipho spent 4 months in hospital and is back at home with his family. He is very happy with his outcome. Ivy is his wife.

Wife
When I saw him for the first time I was very very shock. Because I did not know if he was going to survive, but after 5 days I saw the difference. I think the new treatment helped him very much.

V/O
The other method of creating new skin that is used extensively overseas is by cloning healthy skin cells to grow skin grafts as they did with Pippie Kruger who we featured in 2012.
The difference with Andreone’s method is the cost.

Mac
“Pippie Kruger was well over a million.”

Andreone
“Well over a million.”

V/O
Andreone’s costs are substantially cheaper at R10 000. With the 19 people that he has helped he has also reduced the length of pain that they would have felt.

Nikki
Many of us have burnt our finger and it is sore.What is unquantified is the pain, whether it be an adult or a child will feel then when they are back in their community and they look diiferent they are not the same. What is never talked about is the pain that the health care professionals feel. The nurses that day in and day out treat these patients.
So it is pain on a multitude of levels.

V/O
And for Andreone, it is the pain of not being able to help more.



Sipho
Every pain is now gone. But after one year I think I am going to be OK.

Promo 1 x 10 secs
Possibly a world first , Inkhosi Albert Luthuli Hospital is pioneering a new way of treating severe burn wounds with spray on skin that helps partients recover faster.

Promo 2 x 15 secs

“Boom”

LeeBoy Arendse suffered over 50% full thickness burn wounds when he was set alight last year. His life has been saved through a new technique of spray on skin developed by Dr Andreone at Inkosi Albert Luthuli Central Hospital in Durban.

Promo 3 x 15 secs

Burn injuries are notoriously difficult to treat and the healing process is almost always long and painful. Dr Andreone in KZN has developed a method which sprays skin cells and platelet-rich fibrine onto the exposed flesh and it is helping patients recover faster.


Promo 4 x 30 secs

Burn statistics are very high in SA. It’s estimated that in KwaZulu-Natal alone around 7000 people suffer life-threatening burn injuries every year. But state healthcare can only treat a few hundred. Now, a new procedure which sprays skin cells and platelet-rich fibrine onto burn injuries could mean more patients can be treated in a shorter period of time.

The difference with Andreone’s method is the cost. Mac “Pippie Kruger was well over a million.” Andreone “Well over a million.” V/O Andreone’s costs are substantially cheaper at R10 000. With the 19 people that he has helped he has also reduced the length of pain that they would have felt. Nikki Many of us have burnt our finger and it is sore.What is unquantified is the pain, whether it be an adult or a child will feel then when they are back in their community and they look diiferent they are not the same. What is never talked about is the pain that the health care professionals feel. The nurses that day in and day out treat these patients. So it is pain on a multitude of levels. V/O And for Andreone, it is the pain of not being able to help more. Sipho Every pain is now gone. But after one year I think I am going to be OK. Promo 1 x 10 secs Possibly a world first , Inkhosi Albert Luthuli Hospital is pioneering a new way of treating severe burn wounds with spray on skin that helps partients recover faster. Promo 2 x 15 secs “Boom” LeeBoy Arendse suffered over 50% full thickness burn wounds when he was set alight last year. His life has been saved through a new technique of spray on skin developed by Dr Andreone at Inkosi Albert Luthuli Central Hospital in Durban. Promo 3 x 15 secs Burn injuries are notoriously difficult to treat and the healing process is almost always long and painful. Dr Andreone in KZN has developed a method which sprays skin cells and platelet-rich fibrine onto the exposed flesh and it is helping patients recover faster. Promo 4 x 30 secs Burn statistics are very high in SA. It’s estimated that in KwaZulu-Natal alone around 7000 people suffer life-threatening burn injuries every year. But state healthcare can only treat a few hundred. Now, a new procedure which sprays skin cells and platelet-rich fibrine onto burn injuries could mean more patients can be treated in a shorter period of time.

metadata.Further information: Dr Alessandro Andreone There are very few statistics but it is estimated that there are between 10 000 – 13 000 people that are burnt in KZN every year. About 6 000 – 7000 of them need hospital admission. Inkhosi Albert Lithuli has the only dedicated burns unit and they can only treat 700 patients a year. What happens to the other 5000 patients. Dr Alessandro Andreone has been working in the burns unit for 8 years now. For most people the doctors are able to do a skin graft when a patient comes in with burn wounds. However there are some that come in with burns that are so extensive that they do not have enough skin on their body to cover the area. In overseas countries they rely on cadaver skin. Nikki Allorto who works at Edendale Hospital also looks after wounds at her hospital but there are cultural reasons why the idea of a skin bank has not taken traction. Dr Andreone has been grappling with trying to devise new methods of reducing the time that patients stay in the burns unit to make way for new patients. Recently Carte Blanche featured “Pippie” Kruger the three-year-old burn victim from Limpopo who has made front-page headlines over the past month because of a ¬revolutionary skin transplant operation for which the skin was grown from her own cells in a laboratory in the United States. It was the first time the procedure was performed in Africa. The cost of this technology was approximately a R 1 000 000 and according to Dr Andreone the results are not very successful as the epithelial layer is very thin and it can break. Especially in areas of high friction. Liboy is a labourer in KZN. He was leaving work with his toolbox and 3 men approached him and attacked him to steal his toolbox. Before they left him they lit his clothes on fire and left him to burn. Luckily he was only 2 km away from his employers residence and walked there with 70 % burns on his body. They rushed him to Albert Lithuli. Luckily Dr Andreone was on duty. They removed the burnt flesh and had to put a steralising layer of bovine collagen to protect the exposed flesh. Dr Looking for an alternative way to treat patients, Andreone is Italian and had been researching medical journals and found two machines in Italy that he wanted to experiment with. The machines were not designed for burns applications but he thought that they may be able to work. In Liboy’s case he had enough flesh to create a mesh to cover most of his chest. But how could they get the skin to grow in the holes of the mesh. The Vivostat is a machine that is used in neurosurgery and it extracts fibren from the platelet rich plasma it can extract from blood. This is used to stop bleeding or leaking in brain operations. The Rigenera machine is something that looks like a small electric blender. In a saline solution the doctor places about 2 cm squared of skin into the jug. This blends it so that the skin cells breaks down. Dr Andreone took these cells and put them in the platelet rich plasma and sprayed the mixture onto Liboy’s wounds. To his surprise the wounds started healing very quickly. A process that should have taken 2 months took as little as two weeks. Mr Naidoo was working on his car over the weekend and he did not realise that there was a petrol spill and the petrol had spilt onto the bottom of his pants. He lit a cigarette and his pants caught on fire burning virtually all the skin off his feet. He was rushed to a regional hospital but although they dressed his wounds he was unable to get proper treatment for 2 months. It is obvious how painful burn wounds are. Eventually because his wounds were not healing he was transferred to Albert Lithuli and Dr Andreone tried his new method on him. Withing a couple of weeks the wounds had healed completely. (There is still scar tissue but they are not open weeping wounds). Dr Andreone has treated 8 patients with this method and it seems to be working very well. They have submitted a paper in the Internation Burns Journal and it will be published in 6 weeks time. Both case studies are willing to talk to us. I can interview Dr Andreone, his boss Dr Daan den Hollander and an independent person who has looked at the work. They have also been nominated for a provincial award for the most inventive new medical technique. This method does not only reduce the time that the patient takes to heal, the cost in comparison to epithelial cell culture is a lot less. By getting more patients out of the unit quicker they weill be able to see more patients. What was also interesting was that all of the patients were not there for paraffin burns or accidents as I had imagined, they were all victims of assault where someone had deliberately tried to burn them.
